newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Death and revenge stalk London art exhibition.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Death and revenge stalk London art exhibition.

text.p: London's Summer Exhibition is a highlight of British artistic life, a rare chance for amateur artists to hang their works alongside the professionals in the august surroundings of the Royal Academy.

Critics are often dismissive about the show but it remains a key date in the social season, triggering a migration by the remnants of genteel England from the provinces for a day of cultural fulfilment in the capital.

But this year the Miss Marple lookalikes have been distracted from the pastel shades and rural scenes by a tale of sudden death, revenge and dark threats that has sent a tremor through the arts world.
The epicentre of the exhibition, and the furore surrounding it, is a work by R.B. Kitaj called "Sandra Three" which occupies a whole wall in one of the Academy's high-ceilinged galleries.
Labelled an "avant-garde magazine" by the artist, it is in truth an artistic dagger aimed at the hearts of Kitaj's bitter enemies -- the critics.
"Never in the 230-odd years of RA Summer Exhibitions has such a diatribe been staged," said William Feaver, critic of the Observer newspaper.
Kitaj's huge work is the third in a series of projects he has aimed at the critics he holds responsible for the death of his wife, Sandra Fisher.

Inspired by Manet's "The Execution of Maximilian", it carries a one million pound ($1.63 million) price tag and features Manet as one of the firing squad shooting the gaping-mouthed critics, bloated with envy and bile.

"This curious amalgam of invective, painting, drawing and quotation is a splenetic memorial to Fisher and an accusatory document aimed at what Kitaj sees as the anti-Semitic, xenophobic, and even murderous coven of art critics who derided his retrospective," said Adrian Searle in the Guardian.
WIFE'S DEATH

Fisher, also an artist, died of a brain haemorrhage during a Kitaj retrospective at London's Tate Gallery in 1994 -- an honour for a living artist -- which attracted extremely harsh reviews even by the bitchy standards of the capital's critics.

Kitaj was accused of pure vanity and of being the great pretender, constipated, fake and a purveyor of pastiche and "wretched adolescent trash". One said he would not rate even a footnote in the history of art.
Devastated by the attacks, Kitaj, an American who had made London his home for many years, flew home to visit his 84-year-old mother in Los Angeles.
No sooner had he arrived, than he learnt his wife was desperately ill. He flew back to London and two days later she died aged 47.

Kitaj was inconsolable -- his first wife had committed suicide in the 1960s. "They wounded me, they tried to kill me and they got her instead," he said at the time. A reclusive man, he chose to exact revenge with his talent.
"It was not art criticism but art hatred of a very personal kind, real resentment by sick hacks full of hate and self-hate," he said recently.
His campaign started at the 1996 Summer Exhibition when Kitaj showed "The Critic Kills", a collage which served as a tribute to his late wife and an attack on his critics.
The 1996 painting was the "first issue of an irregular art journal called Sandra", Kitaj said at the time, and in Paris at the turn of the year he issued a magazine named "Sandra Two".

Now "Sandra Three" has arrived, timed to coincide with Kitaj's decision to leave Britain for good. His work was the winner of the award for the exhibition's most distinguished work but it is clear such praise did nothing to ease the 64-year-old's pain.
Kitaj still maintains Fisher "died under enemy fire" from "pathetic, sick, meagre hacks". In two interviews last month, he also showed that he was increasingly interested in the concept of revenge.

"I have begun to study the incredible and noble history of Revenge Tragedy, from the Greeks to 'Hamlet' to Raymond Chandler to Clint Eastwood. And that's a new direction among many directions I wish to pursue, God willing," Kitaj said.

The objects of his loathing seem generally unconcerned that one of "Sandra Three's" images is titled "The Killer-Critic Assassinated By His Widower" and have given Kitaj's latest work another dose of bitter medicine.

"It lacks merit as a piece of art, or any spark of power as polemic. It's just sad and silly and talentless," said A.A. Gill in the Sunday Times. Others expressed sadness that Kitaj could not shake off his obsession.

But one critic said the artist should be feared more than pitied. The Daily Telegraph's Richard Dorment said he had criticised Kitaj's work many years ago and had been the recipient of hate mail so frightening that his wife had thought of calling in the police.

"I strongly feel that the picture in the RA was painted by a man under severe psychological pressure. Perhaps writing menacing letters and painting works like it are his ways of letting off steam. But can one be certain?"
